answer.rationale: The strongest signal is temporal: a release landed 2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90m ago. That ordering makes the release the leading suspect, and rollback is the only candidate that addresses a cause rather than a symptom. I verify memory_b1 because it is the only inherited record that directly supports rollback, and its summary is thin in exactly the ways that matter here: it says the checkout error spike cleared and the prior build was stable, but not whether that incident involved the write path, whether traffic was at peak, or whether the rollback required a schema/state reversal. If the archived record shows the day-18 rollback was a low-traffic, read-path, stateless revert, its transfer to a peak-settlement write-heavy window is weak and I should hold. Rejected alternatives, and why: regional_failover (memory_b2) is superficially attractive because the degradation is confined to the primary region, but failover during peak heavy writes is the single most likely path to losing customer writes via replication lag on an already-degraded primary — it directly contradicts the primary objective, and memory_b2's March incident was a latency event with no stated write-loss exposure. add_capacity (memory_b3) worked when the driver was pre-known surge volume; here volume is expected peak while the anomaly is a new release, so capacity likely masks the regression and burns the one window. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) fits an external dependency failure; this is internal and failing fast on the write path at settlement peak sheds exactly the writes we must not lose. route_read_replicas (memory_b5) relieves read contention, but the degradation is on writes, so it treats the wrong path. Downstream risk: any of these five choices becomes a precedent in this memory, and a success here would be consolidated as 'rollback is right when a release precedes latency' — a rule that would misfire on infrastructure or dependency-driven degradations. Scale is deliberately small and guarded, consistent with memory_b6's evidence that staged cohorts surface regressions within an hour: roll back a bounded cohort first, watch write p99 and write-success rate, and treat non-recovery as disconfirmation rather than a reason to widen. I am not confident the release is causal — the 30m gap between deploy and onset is unexplained and could indicate a slow-building resource leak or an unrelated primary-region fault; I want the guarded step to be able to tell me I am wrong before I commit broadly.
